content.text: Have you ever wondered why bridges have gaps at their joints, why overhead power lines sag more in summer, or why a glass jar lid becomes easier to open after running it under hot water? All of these observations are explained by a single phenomenon: thermal expansion. When substances are heated, they generally expand, and when they are cooled, they contract. This behaviour has profound implications for engineering, construction, and everyday life.
In this lesson, we will explore why materials expand when heated, how much they expand, and the many practical applications and problems that arise from thermal expansion.

Thermal expansion is explained by the kinetic particle model. When a substance is heated, its particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate more vigorously (in solids) or move faster (in liquids and gases). As particles vibrate or move with greater amplitude, they push their neighbours further away. The average distance between particles increases, and the material expands.
It is important to remember that the particles themselves do not get bigger. The increased spacing between particles is what causes the overall expansion of the material.

Solids expand the least of the three states of matter when heated, because the particles are tightly held by strong forces of attraction. However, even small amounts of expansion can cause significant effects in large structures.
Solids can expand in three ways:
The amount by which a solid expands depends on:
: a longer object expands more than a shorter one made of the same material
: a larger temperature increase causes more expansion
: different materials expand by different amounts for the same temperature change

Liquids generally expand more than solids when heated, because the forces between particles in a liquid are weaker, allowing particles to move further apart more easily. Liquids undergo volume expansion only (since they have no fixed shape, linear and area expansion are not meaningful concepts).

The expansion of liquids is applied in liquid-in-glass thermometers. When the temperature rises, the liquid (mercury or alcohol) in the bulb expands and rises up the narrow tube. The narrow bore of the tube makes even small volume changes produce a noticeable change in the length of the liquid column.

Gases expand far more than solids or liquids for the same temperature change. This is because the forces between gas particles are negligible, so there is almost no resistance to particles moving further apart when they gain kinetic energy.

Expansion Joints in Bridges and Roads

Bridges and long sections of road have expansion joints, which are small gaps that allow the structure to expand in hot weather without buckling or cracking. Without these joints, the enormous forces generated by thermal expansion would cause serious structural damage.

A bimetallic strip is made of two different metals bonded together. Since different metals have different coefficients of expansion, the strip bends when heated. The metal with the higher coefficient of expansion is on the outside of the curve.
: The strip bends when the temperature changes, making or breaking an electrical circuit. This can be used to control heating systems, irons, and ovens.
: The strip bends when heated by fire, completing a circuit that triggers the alarm.
: A coiled bimetallic strip uncoils as the temperature rises, turning a pointer on a dial.

Liquid-in-glass thermometers rely on the expansion of a liquid (usually mercury or coloured alcohol) when heated. The liquid expands from a bulb into a narrow capillary tube, and the height of the liquid column indicates the temperature.
A thin-walled glass bulb to allow rapid heat transfer
A narrow bore (capillary tube) to make small expansions easily visible
A uniform bore for a linear scale
A vacuum above the liquid to prevent pressure effects

In engineering, thermal expansion is used to create very tight joints. A metal rivet or ring is heated so that it expands, then placed in position. As it cools and contracts, it grips extremely tightly. This technique, called shrink fitting, is used to fit metal tyres onto train wheels, for example.

Power lines are hung with some slack (they sag slightly between poles). This allows them to contract in cold weather without snapping. In hot weather, the lines expand and sag more, but this is designed into the system.

Older railway tracks were laid in short sections with small gaps between them (you could hear the characteristic "clickety-clack" as the train wheels crossed the gaps). These gaps allowed the tracks to expand in hot weather. Modern continuously welded rails are laid under tension so they can accommodate temperature changes without gaps, but extreme heat can still cause buckling.

If a material is heated unevenly, different parts expand at different rates. This can cause internal stresses that lead to cracking. Pouring boiling water into a thick glass beaker can cause it to crack because the inside expands while the outside remains cool. Pyrex glass has a very low coefficient of expansion, making it resistant to thermal shock.
Large concrete structures like motorways, airport runways, and buildings must include expansion joints. Without them, the concrete would crack and buckle during temperature changes.
Long pipelines (for gas, oil, or hot water) must include expansion loops or flexible joints. A straight pipeline heated by hot fluid would expand and buckle if it were rigidly fixed at both ends.

Misconception 2: "A hole in a metal plate gets smaller when heated"

Actually, a hole in a metal plate gets bigger when the plate is heated. Every part of the metal expands, including the material around the hole. Think of it as the whole plate being scaled up uniformly. The hole expands as if it were filled with the same metal.

While thermal expansion can cause problems if not accounted for, it is also extremely useful. Bimetallic strips, thermometers, shrink fitting, and hot-air balloons all rely on thermal expansion.
